stories.topic: No Highways in India Before His PhD
stories.summary: Ajay notes that before he first went abroad to do a PhD, he had never seen a highway in India — there was not a single one, nor a metro system. This was the material reality of the country in which post-1945 development theorists were arguing about capital stock and technology transfer.
stories.insight: A vivid datum on how recent India's infrastructure story is. The 'capital stock' deficit that the Solow model treated as the central problem was, at the time, a real and visible thing — but fixing it didn't deliver development, which is the whole puzzle this episode is built around.

stories.summary: Growing up, Ajay heard endless rhetoric — including UN bodies like UNIDO and UNCTAD — about rich countries hoarding 'secret runes' of technical knowledge that poor countries needed transferred to them. His father told him this was completely wrong: all the knowledge is in the books, in the papers; you buy the machine and read the manual; patents release knowledge into the public domain. The burden is ours, not theirs.
stories.insight: A formative anti-victimhood frame. The story rich countries told themselves — and which poor countries believed — about secret hoarded knowledge was self-serving fiction on both sides. The brain power and discipline to read manuals is the actual gating step, not state-to-state diplomacy.

stories.topic: The Blue Jeans Factory in Bangalore
stories.summary: One of Ajay's happiest moments of recent months was visiting an Arvind Limited blue jeans factory outside Bangalore. The people there are fully connected to the global state of the art — they know every machine, do careful ROI calculations, travel to China, Taiwan, Europe to buy them, read the manuals, and deploy them. There is no technical or knowledge barrier holding back productivity in India.
stories.insight: A specific, hopeful counterexample to the lazy 'we lack technology' explanation for Indian poverty. If a single jeans factory can operate at the global frontier, the bottleneck on national development is not knowledge — it is something else (institutions, policy, the firm-level environment).

stories.topic: Early South Korean Bureaucrats Looked Up to India
stories.summary: There are stories of early South Korean government functionaries trying to learn from Indian civil service practices. Korea's starting point was abysmal — Seoul was taken and retaken six times in the Korean War; you should think of it as destroyed on the scale of Berlin or Stalingrad or Dresden. Yet South Korea is now an advanced economy and India is not.
stories.insight: The post-1945 'starting line' is a poor predictor of where you end up. Devastation is not destiny — and being looked up to in 1955 is not destiny either. Institutions, ideas, and effort over decades dominate initial conditions.

stories.topic: Two-Thirds of India's Working-Age Population Is Outside the Labour Force
stories.summary: Ajay drops a number that should make any audience fall off their chairs: India's employment rate for ages 16-64 is roughly one-third. For every 100 working-age people, only about 33-35 are working. That means two-thirds of the labour force is sitting outside the mainline market economy.
stories.insight: When the most basic input of the Solow growth model — labour — is being used at one-third capacity, no amount of capital or technology will deliver development. The puzzle of Indian poverty isn't 'where does growth come from?' but 'why aren't existing inputs getting used?'

stories.topic: The Leopard That Almost Attacked Them
stories.summary: Mid-recording on the mountain, the location had to be shifted. As Amit narrates: 'a leopard attacked us, or almost attacked us. It came close and we said, Leopard, Leopard, Mr. Leopard, why are you attacking us? And the leopard said, I smell a Bengali economist.' They finished the episode the next morning.
stories.insight: A warming, very-EIE production aside that doubles as a punchline on their long-running 'Bengali economist' bit (Amit is Bengali, Ajay is the economist — together they jokingly form one). Even shoots can be interrupted by wildlife; episodes, like development, are long journeys.

stories.summary: Amit recalls writing a column arguing that one of the great indicators of women's empowerment in India is a rising divorce rate — because it means women are being empowered to walk out of bad marriages. The column got him a lot of heat, but he stands by it.
stories.insight: A clean illustration of the 'seen vs unseen' lens applied to a social statistic. The seen: divorce as breakdown. The unseen: divorce as exit option, which is empowerment. A society that traps women in bad marriages with low divorce is not 'doing better' than one with rising divorce rates.

stories.topic: The Plea for No Oil Under India
stories.summary: Ajay 'earnestly prays for my country that there will never be a windfall found under the ground in India.' Middle-East-style oil wealth gives you GDP growth without the package of development — the people, the institutions, the freedoms — that we actually want. Saudis are rich and yet, as Ajay notes, most live what most of us would call 'a pretty terrible life.'
stories.insight: Resource curse, in one prayer. The whole point of development is the flourishing of the people, not the size of the government's bank account. A windfall short-circuits the long, painful process by which firms, society and the state co-evolve into something humane.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic: The Art and Science of Economic Policy
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Kelkar and Shah's textbook-but-readable treatise on Indian economic policy, public choice, and the art of state design.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a masterful book that lays out a fundamental framework. Ajay frames it as the book they would send back in a time machine to Jawaharlal Nehru — diagnosing where the big-developmental-state idea went wrong and how to design a state where coercive power is 'cladded like a nuclear reactor' so it can be safely converted into welfare.

recommendations.item: Lant Pritchett's key works (papers, blog posts and podcast episodes)
recommendations.creator: Lant Pritchett
recommendations.context: Pritchett's body of work on national development, the failure of mainstream development economics, and the empirics of growth versus redistribution.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls his work eye-opening and absolutely brilliant — built on hardcore real-world data, not intentions. Two papers in particular underwrite the episode: that ~99% of cross-country variation in poverty rates is explained by median income, and that economic growth is both necessary and sufficient for development.

recommendations.item: The Elusive Quest for Growth
recommendations.creator: William Easterly
recommendations.context: Easterly's classic on the repeated failures of post-WWII development thinking.
recommendations.reason: Essential reading for understanding where development economics often goes wrong — particularly the failures of top-down approaches and the unintended consequences of expert interventions.

recommendations.item: The White Man's Burden
recommendations.creator: William Easterly
recommendations.context: Easterly's critique of foreign aid as a vehicle for development.
recommendations.reason: Companion to Elusive Quest, on why decades of aid haven't moved the needle on national development — and how the philanthropy industry's incentives push it toward attributability rather than impact.

recommendations.item: The Tyranny of Experts
recommendations.creator: William Easterly
recommendations.context: Easterly on the technocratic, paternalist model of development and its costs.
recommendations.reason: Rounds out the Easterly trilogy as a critique of expert-led, freedom-light models of development that have failed across the poor world.

recommendations.item: On the Mechanics of Economic Development
recommendations.creator: Robert E. Lucas
recommendations.context: Lucas's seminal 1988 paper on growth and development.
recommendations.reason: Source of one of the episode's animating quotes: 'Once you start thinking about [development], it's hard to think about anything else,' because the 10x per-capita gap between India and the US is a moral and intellectual problem of the first order.

recommendations.item: The Poverty of Development Economics
recommendations.creator: Deepak Lal
recommendations.context: Lal's classic critique of mid-century development economics.
recommendations.reason: An early, forceful articulation of why the Solow-model-based, planning-heavy approach to development was conceptually broken — pre-figuring the more empirical critiques later refined by Pritchett and Easterly.

recommendations.item: Development Projects Observed
recommendations.creator: Albert O. Hirschman
recommendations.context: Hirschman's deeply observed account of what happens on the ground in development projects.
recommendations.reason: Listed in the show notes as a foundational text for thinking carefully about implementation, side-effects and the gap between development plans and development reality.

recommendations.item: Gambling on Development
recommendations.creator: Stefan Dercon
recommendations.context: Dercon's recent take on why some developing countries take off and most don't.
recommendations.reason: Listed as a key contemporary read on the political economy of development success and failure — complementing the Pritchett–Easterly–Kelkar/Shah core.

recommendations.item: Why Nations Fail
recommendations.creator: Daron Acemoglu and James A. Robinson
recommendations.context: Acemoglu and Robinson on extractive vs inclusive institutions.
recommendations.reason: The institutional-economics canon for understanding why some countries make it to advanced-economy status and most don't.

recommendations.item: The Narrow Corridor
recommendations.creator: Daron Acemoglu and James A. Robinson
recommendations.context: The follow-up volume on the precarious balance between state capacity and societal power.
recommendations.reason: Develops the framework that successful states emerge only when an empowered society and a capable state hold each other in check — directly resonant with the episode's emphasis on society alongside state and firms.

recommendations.item: The Wealth of Nations
recommendations.creator: Adam Smith
recommendations.context: The founding text of economics.
recommendations.reason: Listed in the show notes as the original source for the firm-and-market-centric view of how nations actually become rich.

recommendations.item: Missing in Action
recommendations.creator: Pranay Kotasthane and Raghu S. Jaitley
recommendations.context: Kotasthane and Jaitley's book on the absent Indian state.
recommendations.reason: Referenced in passing as part of the 'state, society, market' framing Amit pushes back on — a useful book even where one disagrees, because it crystallises the dominant frame in Indian public-policy thinking.

recommendations.item: Building State Capability
recommendations.creator: Matt Andrews, Lant Pritchett and Michael Woolcock
recommendations.context: A book of careful measurement and quantification around state capability.
recommendations.reason: Source of the striking finding that during India's great growth episode (1991-2011) state capability actually got worse, even as GDP soared — demonstrating that growth and state quality can run in opposite directions.

recommendations.item: We Should Celebrate Rising Divorce Rates
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's 2008 column arguing that rising divorce rates are an indicator of women's empowerment.
recommendations.reason: The piece that 'got me a lot of heat' — used in the episode to argue that the right indicator of social progress in advanced economies is whether women (and men) have exit options, not whether the institution of marriage looks externally stable.

recommendations.item: The Loneliness of the Indian Woman (Episode 259, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Shrayana Bhattacharya
recommendations.context: Amit's deep-dive episode with Shrayana Bhattacharya.
recommendations.reason: Cited as evidence for the claim that the genders in India 'don't know how to talk to each other' — a society-level deficit of trust capital and collaboration that holds back development.

recommendations.item: The Loneliness of the Indian Man (Episode 303, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Nikhil Taneja
recommendations.context: Companion episode on the male side of the same schism.
recommendations.reason: Together with the previous episode, the pair forms Amit's evidence base for the claim that one of India's deepest barriers to development is the inability of half the country to talk to the other half.

recommendations.item: Rohini Nilekani Pays It Forward (Episode 317, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Rohini Nilekani
recommendations.context: Amit's conversation with Rohini Nilekani.
recommendations.reason: Source of the 'state, society, market' tripartite framing that Amit critiques in this episode — markets, he argues, are not a third pillar but a mechanism by which society expresses its voluntary, positive-sum interactions.

recommendations.item: The Life and Times of the Indian Economy (Episode 387, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Rajeshwari Sengupta
recommendations.context: Deep dive on India's post-independence economic journey.
recommendations.reason: Companion episode for listeners who want the longer story of how India ended up a 1/10th-per-capita country and what its growth episodes looked like up close.

recommendations.item: Demystifying GDP (Episode 130, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Rajeswari Sengupta
recommendations.context: An episode unpacking what GDP measures and what it misses.
recommendations.reason: Linked because the episode uses GDP and per-capita GDP as the unit of measure throughout — Amit acknowledges GDP is imperfect but defends it as the closest single number we have for national prosperity.

recommendations.item: Lant Pritchett Is on Team Prosperity (Episode 379, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Lant Pritchett
recommendations.context: Amit's long-form conversation with Lant Pritchett.
recommendations.reason: The episode where Pritchett's full case — growth as necessary and sufficient, the failure of kinky development, the distortion of the field — is laid out at length. Amit treats it as required listening for anyone wanting to go deeper.

recommendations.item: Where Did Development Economics Go Wrong? (Ideas of India)
recommendations.creator: Lant Pritchett with Shruti Rajagopalan
recommendations.context: Pritchett's diagnosis of the field on Shruti Rajagopalan's podcast.
recommendations.reason: Companion long-form interview that goes deeper into the institutional and incentive distortions behind development economics' decline.

recommendations.item: Reforming Development Economics (Ideas of India)
recommendations.creator: Lant Pritchett with Shruti Rajagopalan
recommendations.context: Pritchett on what an honest, useful development economics would look like.
recommendations.reason: The constructive sequel to the 'where did it go wrong' conversation — together they form a complete reading of Pritchett's reform agenda.

recommendations.item: Economic growth is enough and only economic growth is enough
recommendations.creator: Lant Pritchett with Addison Lewis
recommendations.context: Pritchett's data-driven case for growth as the dominant lever for poverty reduction.
recommendations.reason: Linked from the show notes as one of the 'eye-opening' Pritchett papers underwriting Amit's claim that 99% of poverty-rate variance is explained by median income, not by anti-poverty programmes.

recommendations.item: National Development Delivers: And How! And How?
recommendations.creator: Lant Pritchett
recommendations.context: Pritchett on what national development is and how it actually shows up in human welfare.
recommendations.reason: The paper that introduces the 'national development versus kinky development' distinction Amit relies on heavily in the second half of the episode.

recommendations.item: What I, as a development economist, have been actively 'for'
recommendations.creator: Lant Pritchett
recommendations.context: Pritchett's positive statement of his own development agenda.
recommendations.reason: The constructive companion to his many critiques — what is to be done, in his own words. Linked in the show notes as a key Pritchett primer.

recommendations.item: Why Freedom Matters (Episode 10 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An earlier EIE episode on why freedom — economic, social, political — is the actual goal.
recommendations.reason: Linked because this episode reframes development as not merely per-capita GDP but the full package of freedoms (mind, bedroom, public square) that advanced economies have.

recommendations.item: The India Uncut Newsletter
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's Substack newsletter.
recommendations.reason: Self-recommendation in the show notes — the channel through which Amit develops many of the ideas referenced here.

recommendations.item: The Art of Clear Writing
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's online writing course.
recommendations.reason: Standard self-recommendation listed in the show notes — relevant here because clear thinking and clear writing are how the development-economics fog gets lifted.

recommendations.item: XKDR Forum (YouTube channel)
recommendations.creator: XKDR Forum
recommendations.context: Ajay's research organisation's YouTube channel.
recommendations.reason: Listed in show notes as the home of Ajay's longer-form research output on the questions raised in this episode.

core_ideas.concept: The 10x Gap as the Defining Question
core_ideas.explanation: Indian per-capita GDP (PPP-adjusted) is roughly one-tenth of the United States'. Not 10 percent gap, but a factor of ten. Once you sit with that number, it becomes hard to think about anything else — the difference between the two is a hot bath in winter, mosquito screens, protein for a stunted child, and a thousand other basic dignities. Development economics is the field that takes the 10x gap as its central, animating puzzle.
core_ideas.quote: Once you start thinking about [development], it's hard to think about anything else.

core_ideas.concept: The Solow-Solow-Swan Inheritance and Why It Failed
core_ideas.explanation: Post-WWII development thinking inherited the Solow-Swan growth model: per-capita output is a function of capital stock per capita and productivity (treated as 'the manuals' — machines, technology, scientific knowledge). The development-economics intuition was: pile on capital, get the manuals, and you're done. Decades on, this is empirically wrong. India has plentiful labour, infinite global capital, and full access to every manual and machine — yet per-capita GDP is still 1/10th of the US. The bottleneck must be elsewhere.

core_ideas.concept: Failure Is the Norm, Success the Exception
core_ideas.explanation: Of all the countries that were poor in 1945, only four have made it to advanced-economy status: South Korea, Taiwan, Israel and Chile. More than a hundred have not. Development is statistically rare, not inevitable — and the early post-war optimism that growth was 'baked in' (a child becomes an adult, a puppy becomes a dog) is precisely the wrong frame. Treat development like climbing Mount Everest: dangerous, statistically unlikely, and only achievable if you take it seriously.
core_ideas.quote: Statistically, development doesn't happen. It is the exception rather than the norm.

core_ideas.concept: All Advanced Economies Look Alike (Anna Karenina, Inverted)
core_ideas.explanation: Tolstoy said all happy families are alike. Ajay generalises: poor countries are wildly heterogeneous (India, Burma, Cambodia, South Africa are all unlike one another), but advanced economies share a striking common package — prosperous liberal democracies, freedom of speech and press, rule of law, world-class firms, separation of church and state, declining religiosity, the state as agent and not principal. Not one advanced economy is authoritarian. The package is the destination.

core_ideas.concept: Growth Is Necessary and Sufficient (the Pritchett Result)
core_ideas.explanation: Lant Pritchett's empirical work shows that ~99% of cross-country variation in the poverty rate is explained by a single number: median income. Inequality, redistribution, welfare programmes — all account for roughly 1% of the story. A separate Pritchett paper argues growth is both necessary and sufficient for development: with growth you get there; without growth you don't. Therefore the moral, evidence-based imperative for a poor country is: fix the middle. Lift mean and median income. Poverty falls as a side-effect.
core_ideas.quote: 99% of the variance of the poverty rate is explained by growth, not by the obsessions of people who are taking interest in poverty directly.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's reframing of the development agenda into three pillars: (1) the emergence of a high-productivity economy, i.e. firms that can match the global frontier; (2) the emergence of state capability, i.e. a state that can do a few things well rather than many things badly, with rule of law as its connective tissue; (3) the emergence of a political system in which the state is the agent of the people rather than their ma-baap. Rule of law is not a fourth pillar but the raw material of the second and third.

core_ideas.concept: Society as the Hidden Fourth Variable
core_ideas.explanation: Beyond firms and the state lies society — culture, norms, trust capital, communities, the ability to talk to each other and collaborate. In World Values Survey data, advanced economies report 50-90% generalised trust; India reports about 15%. Low trust capital means problems that could be solved by neighbours talking to each other instead get pushed onto a state too weak to solve them — what Ajay calls 'premature expansion of scope', leading to organisational collapse of the state. One concrete deficit: Indian boys and girls don't know how to talk to each other.
core_ideas.quote: Half the people are on one side, half the people are on the other side. And they can't talk to each other.

core_ideas.concept: Firms Are the Site Where GDP Is Made
core_ideas.explanation: Output is made in firms. Per-capita output of an advanced economy is the per-worker output of its firms — Google, JP Morgan, Toyota, Samsung, TSMC, IKEA — multiplied across the workforce. If you don't put the firm under the microscope, you can't understand development. Yet mainstream development economics treats firms as 'rich people' and looks past them. The seen-vs-unseen lesson: what the firm has done is visible; what bad regulation prevented it from doing is invisible — and probably much larger.

core_ideas.concept: Markets Are a Mechanism of Society, Not a Third Pillar
core_ideas.explanation: Amit pushes back on the popular 'state-society-market' tripartite framing (used by Raghuram Rajan, Rohini Nilekani, Pranay Kotasthane and Raghu Jaitley). The market is not a third entity — it is a mechanism through which society expresses voluntary, positive-sum cooperation: 'a web of double thank-you moments.' Treating markets as a separate pillar lets people demonise them; treating them as society in motion makes the case that hostility to markets is hostility to ordinary people doing things for each other.

core_ideas.concept: Growth and State Capability Can Run in Opposite Directions
core_ideas.explanation: A common error: assume that because GDP grew, the state must have improved. The data say otherwise. Andrews-Pritchett's Building State Capability finds that during India's 1991-2011 growth episode, state capability actually got worse. Larger dollar values being waved at unchanged regulators, judges and bureaucrats overwhelmed checks and balances designed for a smaller economy. So a growth episode contains the seeds of its own end — the state machinery falls behind the economy it is supposed to police. This is one reason developing-economy growth comes in spurts; the UK and US managed 200 years at 3%.

Nehruvian high modernism — the state grabs the people by the scruff of the neck and drags them into development — was the dominant 1947 ideology and is, Ajay argues, alive and well today. Most Indian businesspeople, asked how to fix the country, want the state to do more, not less. Keynes's reminder is the corrective: 'The job of the state is not to do things a little bit better than what private people will do. The job of the state is to do the things that the private sector will not do at all.'

core_ideas.concept: Public Health Is Not Health Care
core_ideas.explanation: Development economics has confused the two. Public health is the population-scale work of fixing water, sanitation, air quality, mosquitoes, antimicrobial resistance, road crashes — the things the private sector won't and can't do. Health care is what happens when you, individually, get malaria and want to be treated; it can largely be provisioned privately. Building primary health centres in every village is a deluded substitute for the actual public-goods work that produces healthy populations.
core_ideas.quote: If you get malaria and you go to get treatment for your malaria, that is health care, that is private. If you think about eradicating mosquitoes so malaria doesn't happen at all, that is a public good and that is what the state should do.

core_ideas.concept: Cladding the Coercive Power of the State
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's metaphor for state design: coercive power is poison, and the state is supposed to be a machine that converts that poison into welfare. Doing this safely requires heavy 'cladding like a nuclear reactor' — checks and balances, formal organisational structures, careful drafting of laws to limit and channel power. Every additional power, every additional dataset, every additional intervention given to the state requires correspondingly more cladding. Premature state legibility — adding power and information without the cladding — is a recipe for state failure.
core_ideas.quote: Our ultimate dream is the state is supposed to be a machine that converts coercive power into welfare.

core_ideas.concept: National Development vs. Kinky Development (and the Streetlight Effect)
core_ideas.explanation: Pritchett's distinction. National development is the hard, indivisible question: how do we raise median per-capita GDP and pull a population out of poverty over decades? Kinky development is what mainstream development economics has retreated to instead — narrow, attributable, tractable interventions like 'do treated mosquito nets reduce malaria?' Amit's metaphor: a drunk searching for his keys under the lamppost not because he dropped them there but because the light is there. Kinky development is the lamppost; national development is the bushes.
core_ideas.quote: I'm looking here because the light is here.

core_ideas.explanation: Why the field went kinky. (1) Philanthropic incentives: philanthropists and especially their staffs need attributable wins, so they fund narrow projects with claimable outcomes, not the indivisible work of national development. (2) Populism: democratic politics rewards visible redistribution ('I gave you 2,000 rupees') over invisible growth-creation ('I made conditions for GDP'). Hence the Robin-Hood / Piketty turn. (3) The frat-boy world of US economics journals: referees demand ironclad causal identification on small questions, killing big-question research and rewarding RCT-fundraising careers. The result: the field stopped asking the questions it exists to answer.

Amit's closing public-policy lesson. Many policies with great intentions deliver opposite outcomes — labour laws meant to protect workers cripple firm growth and therefore hurt workers; anti-poverty programmes consume the political oxygen that growth needs. Outcomes are what matter. Combined with his other plea — think independently, even of your own tribe — this becomes a near-Hayekian discipline: keep checking whether the package of beliefs you've adopted still tracks the world.
core_ideas.quote: We could also be full of shit.

core_ideas.concept: Growth in Spurts, Not in Generations
core_ideas.explanation: Developing economies grow like hares (1991-2011 India), advanced economies grew like tortoises (200 years at 3% in the UK/US — they never faltered). The deep open question is why India can't seem to do sustained growth. One conjecture in the episode: success breeds complacency; the criticism that keeps the state honest atrophies during good years; mismatches between an evolving economy and an unchanged state machinery accumulate; eventually the spurt ends. So the next wave of Indian growth depends not on the economy but on the ideas, knowledge and community needed to fix the state.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit on the natural studio: 'It is the best green screen known to man. It is a natural green screen.' Ajay on the cinematography: their hair light is 'one hundred and fifty million kilometres behind' — i.e., the sun.
The recurring 'Bengali economist' joke — between Amit (Bengali) and Ajay (economist), they jointly form one. Ajay's claim to Bengali-ness: he puts on the jacket first.

The leopard interrupts the shoot. Amit narrates: 'A leopard attacked us, or almost attacked us. It came close and we said, Leopard, Leopard, Mr. Leopard, why are you attacking us? And the leopard said, I smell a Bengali economist.'

Ajay's Mount-Everest metaphor for development: if you tell Amit climbing Everest is 'just a matter of eating enough protein bars', he'll fail. Tell him it's statistically unlikely and he'll train for it. Optimism is the enemy of preparation.

The 'elephant dung cures elephantiasis' image: Ajay's mockery of redistribution-first poverty work — primitive thinkers reasoned that since the words sounded similar, the cure must be elephant dung. Actually, it's antibiotics. So with poverty: the cure isn't fighting poverty directly, it's fixing the median income.
Amit on India's bad labour laws: workers get protected onto unemployment, firms hire on contract, 'and everyone is crippled.'
Amit's plea to readers, after a full hour of confident pronouncements: 'We could also be full of shit.'
'Start at the very beginning' — Amit cues Ajay with the Sound of Music line; Ajay finishes it: 'A very good place to start.'
Robert Lucas's 1988 'On the Mechanics of Economic Development' — the source of the line that once you start thinking about development, it's hard to think about anything else.

Tolstoy, Anna Karenina — 'all happy families are alike, all unhappy families are unhappy in different ways' — used to set up the symmetry that all advanced economies are alike, all poor countries are poor differently.

Keynes on the proper role of the state: 'The job of the state is not to do things a little bit better than what private people will do. The job of the state is to do the things that the private sector will not do at all.'
Gandhi's talisman: for everything the state wants to do, ask what it will do for the poorest person in the land. Invoked as the moral lens behind their growth-first stance.
Macaulay's children — Ajay's nod to the colonial bequest of English-speaking elites who, in the early decades after independence, were supposed to be development's transmission belt.

The Nehru-Mahalanobis 'big developmental state' — the Indian National Congress economic intellectual community of 1947, captured here in caricature: 'India is a wretched poor country... and the state is this noble creature who is going to grab the people by the scruff of the neck and drag the people into development.'
The empty chair for Harold Laski — the old quip that at every Nehru cabinet meeting there was a phantom seat for the Fabian socialist Laski. Amit wishes there had been one for Lant Pritchett instead.

Hayek's The Road to Serfdom — 'an obscure bestseller' in 1947 India, taken less seriously than Laski; the public-choice canon that would later have armed Nehru against his own delusions did not yet exist.

The Battle of Tannenberg (1916) and the Russian defeat by Japan (1905) — Ajay's quick sketch of Russia's appalling early-20th-century starting point, en route to becoming the world's largest land power by 1945. Used to explain why USSR-style state-led development looked attractive in 1947.
Battle scars of Berlin, Stalingrad and Dresden — the analogues Ajay reaches for to convey what Seoul looked like at the end of the Korean War, having been taken and retaken six times.

IKEA as case study — Ajay's invitation to gentle readers: don't just shop at IKEA, walk around the store and admire the company. 'What audacity of conception that you could dream such a business.' A microcosm of what an advanced-economy firm looks like.

Metcalfe's Law — the value of a network is proportional to the square of the number of users. Invoked to describe the Indian English-speaking elite as a network whose power to break tribal identities scales with its size.
Thomas Piketty / The French Revolution — Ajay's shorthand for the long arc of inequality-obsession that, in his telling, has crowded out growth from progressive imaginations.
